summary: This informational memo presents a problem statement for access rate measurement test protocols used with IP Performance Metrics (IPPM). It discusses key aspects such as controlling the packet characteristics on the tested path and states requirements for such a protocol.

eli5.summary: How do you measure how fast an internet connection really is? This note explains why that is hard and what a good measuring tool needs.

questions: how to measure access rate ippm
how to measure internet access rate
subtitle: What a protocol must be able to do to measure how fast an Internet access link really is.

tldr.problem: People choosing an Internet access service want comparable measurements of access rate, but the measurement methods and test protocols in use differ widely, and access links are often asymmetric and slower than the rest of the network.
tldr.mechanism: The memo states the problem for active measurement of access rate and lists what a test protocol must support, such as packet ensemble generation, control of packet sizes and rates, and asymmetric rates in each direction.
tldr.outcome: It is a problem statement, not a protocol: it deliberately does not specify a measurement method, and notes that the IETF test protocols it cites do not yet offer asymmetric packet sizes in two-way testing.

today: RFC 7497 is an Informational RFC published in April 2015. It has not been obsoleted or updated according to the unit metadata, and it remains a problem statement rather than a protocol specification.

sections.title: The Access Rate Problem
sections.content:
RFC 7497 is an informational memo from the IETF's IP Performance Metrics (IPPM) work. It presents one problem statement: how test protocols can measure the access rate of an Internet connection. It states that many other rate measurement scenarios are possible.

Subscribers compare access alternatives such as fibre, copper and radio, and standardized measurements can be the basis for comparison. The RFC notes that the problem is being approached with many different measurement methods, so there is a need to coordinate measurements and to test control protocols.
sections.eli5: People want to compare internet connections fairly. That only works if everyone measures speed the same way.

sections.title: Purpose and Scope
sections.content:
The scope is test protocols that measure access rate on production networks. The RFC names RFC 4656 and RFC 5357 as relevant test protocols, and says the problem is stated generally enough for any existing test protocol, such as RFC 6812.

The focus is the access portion of the network, where rates are often several orders of magnitude lower than in the aggregation and core. Asymmetric access rates in the two directions are prevalent. The statement assumes the likely bottleneck is next to the remote measurement device or within one or two router or switch hops of it. A second use case is leased capacity from another operator, such as mobile backhaul, which the RFC calls the aggregated leased-network case.

Only active measurement is covered: synthetic traffic dedicated to testing, not measurement of user traffic. Both In-Service testing (user traffic present) and Out-of-Service testing (for example service commissioning or planned maintenance) are in scope. Solving the protocol specification and standardizing measurement methods are explicit non-goals.

Test traffic may be treated differently from user traffic. Packet length, IP addresses, transport protocol and port numbers can all affect Equal-Cost Multipath (ECMP) routing, so a solution may need to closely emulate user traffic.
sections.eli5: The note is about testing the last stretch of road to your house, which is usually the narrowest. It does not pick a tool; it only says what the problem is.

sections.title: Active Measurement Roles
sections.content:
Active tests intrude on user performance, especially In-Service tests. Users of such protocols MUST respect the traffic constraints that keep test traffic from skewing results or congesting the access link. Out-of-Service tests that share part of the path with In-Service traffic must respect the same constraints.

The measurement architecture may be one-way (RFC 4656) or two-way (RFC 5357). Scale and complexity favor two-way, with a low-complexity device at the user end. Because rates are often asymmetric, the system MUST be able to evaluate each direction, so both end devices must be able to launch test streams and collect results in both directions.

Three roles are described:

  • SENDER: generates test packet streams, at the user end or elsewhere.
  • RECEIVER: collects the streams and makes the measurements.
  • REPORTER: turns delivered packet rates into results, and may be combined with another role.
sections.eli5: One side throws balls, the other side catches and counts them, and someone writes down the score. The test must not be so rough that it bothers the people using the connection.

sections.title: Stream Categories and Variables
sections.content:
The protocol must serve test stream generation and measurement (SENDER and RECEIVER). Analyzing results is outside scope. The RFC sorts stream generation into four categories: packet pairs, multiple streams of packet pairs, packet ensembles, and packet chirps. The test protocol SHALL support packet ensemble generation, because that appears to minimize the demands on measurement accuracy. The other categories are OPTIONAL.

For every supported category the protocol MUST be able to specify, control and generate variable payload lengths, stream or ensemble lengths in packets, IP header markings, UDP or TCP transport with variable port numbers (TCP only for two-way architectures), and the number of pairs, ensembles or streams in a session. Changing these during a session is OPTIONAL.

For TCP, the sender must act as an open-loop sender: well-formed headers, controlled rates and spacings, and continuing to send despite control indications except receive-window exhaust. Each UDP test packet MUST be measured consistently with the singleton methods of RFC 2679 and RFC 2680.
sections.eli5: The tool should be able to send packets in different patterns, like a steady drip, a quick burst, or a growing rush, and change how big and how many they are.

sections.title: Control and Generation Requirements
sections.content:
In summary the test protocol must support: communicating all test variables to the SENDER and RECEIVER, results collection in a one-way architecture, remote device control for one-way and two-way architectures, and asymmetric packet rates in a two-way architecture (or coordinated one-way tests with the same effect). Control and generation of asymmetric rates in a two-way architecture is REQUIRED.

Two-way architectures are RECOMMENDED to support both asymmetric and symmetric packet sizes, since packet size often matters. Asymmetric size control is indicated when, for example, a link has different capacity in each direction, a link groups packets into frames, a device's capacity depends on header processing, or the target application sends MTU-size packets one way and an ACK stream the other way. Symmetric sizes alone are acceptable when none of the listed conditions hold.

The protocol SHOULD enable measuring the capacity metric of RFC 5136, out-of-service, in-service or both. Other metrics are OPTIONAL.
sections.eli5: Because download and upload speeds are often different, the tool must be able to test each direction separately, with different sizes of packets if needed.

sections.title: Security and Operational Notes
sections.content:
The security considerations of any active measurement of live networks apply (see RFC 4656 and RFC 5357). If a proprietary service level agreement were leaked during rate measurement, that could be a serious issue, so test protocols SHOULD NOT convey such information where unauthorized parties could discover it.

Testing creates traffic. Subscribers and authorized users SHOULD obtain the network operator's permission before testing, and a provider or third party SHOULD obtain the subscriber's permission, since tests might temporarily reduce service quality. Occasional short tests with minimal traffic are preferred to frequent transfers of many megabytes. The RFC notes that the current IETF test protocols it cites (RFC 5357 and RFC 6812) lack asymmetric size generation in two-way testing.
sections.eli5: Always ask before running a speed test on someone else's connection, and keep tests small so they do not slow everyone down.

items.label: Packet pairs
items.desc: Fixed intra-pair spacing; fixed or random intervals between pairs.

items.label: Multiple pair streams
items.desc: A range of intra-pair spacing and inter-pair intervals.

items.label: Packet ensembles
items.desc: Fixed ensemble size and spacings, including back-to-back bursts. Required support.

items.label: Packet chirps
items.desc: Inter-packet spacing typically decreases; each pair represents a rate.
